Components of Fitness: Health-related fitness
The five components that reduce disease risk and support daily function
Skill-related fitness
Attributes such as agility, balance, power, and reaction time
Cardiorespiratory endurance
The ability of the heart and lungs to sustain activity
Muscular strength
The greatest force a muscle can exert in one effort
Muscular endurance
The ability to repeat contractions over time without fatigue
Flexibility
The range of motion available at a joint
Body composition
The ratio of lean mass to fat mass in the body
Agility
The ability to change direction quickly and under control
Power
Strength applied rapidly, combining force and speed
Reaction time
How quickly a person responds to a stimulus
Coordination
Using senses and body parts together smoothly
Fitness assessment
A test such as the mile run or push-up test measuring a component
Baseline measurement
A starting score used to track improvement over time
Cardiovascular Training: Aerobic activity
Sustained exercise that relies on oxygen for energy
Maximum heart rate
Estimated as 220 minus age, a rough training reference
Target heart rate zone
Typically 60 to 85 percent of maximum heart rate
Moderate intensity
Effort where you can talk but not sing comfortably
Vigorous intensity
Effort where speaking more than a few words is difficult
Rate of perceived exertion
A subjective scale rating how hard exercise feels
Recovery heart rate
How quickly the pulse falls after exercise, a fitness indicator
Continuous training
Steady effort held for an extended period
Interval training
Alternating hard efforts with recovery periods
High-intensity interval training
Short maximal bursts separated by brief rest
Cross-training
Varying activities to build fitness and reduce overuse injury
Weekly activity guideline
At least 60 minutes of daily activity for teenagers
VO2 max
The maximum rate of oxygen the body can use during exercise
Cardiac output
The volume of blood the heart pumps each minute
Strength Training Principles: Resistance training
Exercise working muscles against an opposing force
Repetition
One complete performance of an exercise movement
Set
A group of repetitions performed consecutively
One-repetition maximum
The heaviest load liftable once with good form
Progressive overload
Gradually increasing demand to force adaptation
Isometric contraction
Muscle tension without a change in length, such as a plank
Isotonic contraction
Muscle contraction through a range of motion
Concentric phase
The shortening phase of a lift, such as curling upward
Eccentric phase
The lengthening phase, where most soreness originates
Compound exercise
A movement working several joints and muscle groups at once
Isolation exercise
A movement targeting a single muscle group
Bodyweight training
Resistance work using only your own mass as load
Rest between sets
Recovery time that determines whether strength or endurance is trained
Spotter
A partner who assists and protects a lifter
Proper form
Technique that maximises benefit and minimises injury risk
Muscle hypertrophy
The growth of muscle fibres in response to training
Flexibility and Mobility: Exercise that increases the range of motion at joints
Holding a stretch position, best performed after activity
Controlled movement through a range of motion, best before activity
Bouncing into a stretch, generally discouraged due to injury risk
A contract-relax technique producing large flexibility gains
The ability to move a joint actively through its full range
The extent of movement possible at a joint
A stretch of the muscles along the back of the thigh
A stretch addressing tightness from prolonged sitting
Self-myofascial release using body weight on a roller
The alignment of the body at rest and in motion
Pushing beyond safe limits, which can strain tissue
Better movement quality, reduced stiffness, and lower injury risk
Team Sports Skills and Rules: Offense and defense
The team attempting to score versus the team preventing scoring
Basketball travelling violation
Moving the pivot foot illegally while holding the ball
Basketball double dribble
Dribbling again after having stopped the dribble
Basketball personal foul
Illegal contact that impedes an opponent
Basketball three-point line
The arc beyond which a made shot scores three points
Soccer offside
Being nearer the goal than the ball and second-last defender when the ball is played
Soccer throw-in
The two-handed overhead restart after the ball crosses the touchline
Soccer yellow and red cards
A caution versus an ejection from the match
Volleyball rotation
Players shifting clockwise after winning serve
Volleyball three-hit rule
A team may contact the ball at most three times before returning it
Volleyball carry violation
Prolonged contact where the ball comes to rest on the hands
Rally scoring
A system awarding a point on every rally regardless of who served
Football down
One of four attempts to advance the ball ten yards
Softball force out
Retiring a runner who must advance by touching the base with the ball
Sportsmanship
Fair play, respect for opponents, and gracious response to outcomes
Teamwork
Coordinated effort where individual roles serve a shared goal
Individual and Lifetime Sports: An activity a person can continue safely into older adulthood
The 15, 30, 40, game sequence with deuce and advantage
A tied score at 40 requiring a two-point margin to win
The exchange of shots between serve and point completion
The expected number of strokes for a skilled player on a hole
One stroke under par versus one stroke over
A practice combining postures, breathing, and focus
A method emphasising core strength and controlled movement
Doing an activity because it is satisfying in itself
Doing an activity for an external reward
Sticking with an activity program over the long run
Nutrition for Performance: Carbohydrate loading
Increasing stored glycogen before an endurance event
Glycogen
The stored carbohydrate that fuels sustained exercise
Pre-exercise meal
A carbohydrate-focused meal eaten a few hours before activity
Recovery nutrition
Carbohydrate and protein consumed soon after training
Protein needs for athletes
Modestly higher than for sedentary people, still met by normal diets
Hydration before activity
Drinking fluids in advance rather than relying on thirst
Dehydration
Fluid loss that reduces performance and raises heat illness risk
Electrolytes
Minerals such as sodium and potassium lost through sweat
Sports drink
A beverage supplying fluid, carbohydrate, and electrolytes
Energy drink risk
High caffeine content that can strain the cardiovascular system
Supplement caution
Products that are loosely regulated and may be contaminated
Weight-cutting dangers
Rapid dehydration practices that risk serious harm
Fueling for growth
Adolescent athletes needing enough calories to support development
Injury Prevention and Safety: A sudden injury such as a sprain or fracture
Damage accumulating from repetitive stress without recovery
A stretched or torn muscle or tendon
Rest, ice, compression, and elevation for soft tissue injury
Inflammation of a tendon from repeated stress
Lower leg pain often from rapid increases in running volume
A brain injury requiring immediate removal from play
The staged process for safely resuming activity after concussion
Gear such as helmets and mouthguards that reduces injury severity
Fluid loss raising the risk of heat exhaustion and heat stroke
A medical emergency with high body temperature and altered mental state
Raising tissue temperature and preparing the nervous system
Scheduled downtime that allows adaptation and prevents overtraining
Declining performance and fatigue from insufficient recovery
Goal Setting and Personal Fitness Plans: Personal fitness plan
A written program matching activities to individual goals
SMART goal
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and timed
Process goal
A goal about actions taken, such as training three times weekly
Outcome goal
A goal about a result, such as running a certain time
Self-assessment
Evaluating current fitness before designing a program
FITT principle in planning
Setting frequency, intensity, time, and type for each component
Periodization
Organising training into phases with varying emphasis
Progress tracking
Recording workouts and measurements to evaluate improvement
Plateau
A stall in progress that signals a need to change the stimulus
Barrier to activity
An obstacle such as time, cost, or access that limits exercise
Realistic expectations
Understanding that meaningful fitness change takes months
Lifelong activity habit
Building routines that persist beyond a class or season
Reassessment
Retesting fitness components to update the plan
